\section{Methods}

\subsection{Overview}

Each pair is assigned to an algorithm (Table~\ref{tab:engines}; Fig.~\ref{fig:overview}). Unit costs follow A*PA2 \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}: band doubling over 256-column tiles of bit-parallel words, pruned on long pairs by the gap-chaining seed heuristic \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}, with near-identical pairs aligned by diagonal transition alone. Gap-affine costs use the wavefront of WFA and BiWFA \citep{MarcoSola2021wfa,MarcoSola2023biwfa}. At unit costs, diagonal transition runs first and hands over once its projected remaining work exceeds the band's and it has spent a twenty-fourth of the band's least work (Section 3.10); its projection, the length and the cost model then choose the next algorithm and its parameters.

At unit, gap-affine and two-piece costs, every engine selects the same alignment among equally good ones, by the backtrace order of WFA2-lib: from the end, an edit is preferred to a match whenever one is optimal, a substitution before a deletion (a letter of \(A\) alone) before an insertion, the second gap piece before the first, and an extension before an opening. This gives WFA2-lib's CIGARs exactly; the default applies it to both sequences reversed, which places every edit as far left as possible, as variant callers normalise indels. Every engine takes the furthest-reaching source or stores per-cell flags under the rule. A gap-affine pair split for the memory limit follows the rule within each piece, and alignments under a substitution matrix follow the traceback order of Gotoh's recurrence.

\subsection{A shorter critical path for Myers' recurrence}

As in Edlib and A*PA2 \citep{Sosic2017edlib,GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}, the query is packed 64 bases per word, and Myers' recurrence \citep{Myers1999bitvector} advances a word by one column. With match mask \(E\), vertical difference masks \(P_v, M_v\) and the incoming negative horizontal difference folded into \(E' = E \lor M_h^{\mathrm{in}}\), A*PA2 computes

\begin{equation}\begin{gathered}
c = (E' \land P_v) + P_v,\\ X_h = (c \oplus P_v) \lor E',\\ P_h = M_v \lor \lnot(X_h \lor P_v),\\ M_h = P_v \land X_h.
\end{gathered}\end{equation}

The horizontal masks \(P_h\) and \(M_h\) determine the vertical masks of the next column, so the path from \(c\) to them lies on the loop-carried chain. Since \((c \oplus P_v) \lor P_v = c \lor P_v\) and \(P_v \land (c \oplus P_v) = P_v \land \lnot c\), the same masks are obtained as

\begin{equation}\begin{gathered}
P_h = M_v \lor \lnot\bigl(c \lor (E' \lor P_v)\bigr),\\ M_h = (P_v \land \lnot c) \lor (P_v \land E'),
\end{gathered}\end{equation}

where \(E' \lor P_v\) and \(P_v \land E'\) do not depend on \(c\) and are computed off the critical path. The vertical update is regrouped in the same way, its negated part computed from \(E\), \(M_v\) and the incoming horizontal difference before \(P_h\) is known. Together the rewrites shorten the loop-carried chain of a single word from 14 to 8 cycles per column. \citet{Myers1999bitvector}, Edlib and A*PA2 use the original form, and we are not aware of a previous description of the regrouped one.

Words occupy the lanes of a vector, staggered by one column, so that the horizontal difference leaving one word enters the next by a lane rotation \citep{Wozniak1997,GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}, on which each column waits. On AVX-512 dinara-align interleaves two eight-word groups, ten columns apart, so that each fills the latency of the other, and bands of two or three words run in general-purpose registers.

\subsection{Band bounds from agreeing estimates}

Band doubling is exact for any initial bound, but its running time depends on how close that bound is to the distance. A computation that has reached cost \(s\) at anti-diagonal \(\rho\) estimates the distance as \(\hat D = s(n+m)/\rho\), which is reliable when edits are spread evenly and too high by orders of magnitude when they gather, as at the ends of nanopore reads. dinara-align takes two estimates, \(\hat D_1\) from a one-ended diagonal transition stopped after eight edits and \(\hat D_2\) from the two-ended search where it handed over. When at least one seed in 32 chains from the origin, the first bound starts 64 above the seed heuristic there. Otherwise it is aimed just above \(\hat D_1\) when the two estimates agree within a third, and failing that, as in A*PA2, it starts at most 256 above the known lower bound and at most doubles until a failed round has crossed an eighth of the columns. A failed round aims the next bound from where it stopped, and the first round estimates again after an eighth, a quarter and a half of the columns. A distance is accepted only within the bound its round ended on, so these rules change only the sequence of bounds and the result stays exact.

Within a round, the band drops the rows at the top and bottom of each tile whose score plus the heuristic exceeds the bound, as A*PA2 does. A score changes by at most one per row and the heuristic by at most its climb \(\gamma\), so a row that exceeds the bound by \(y\) also rules out the next \(\lceil y/(1+\gamma) \rceil - 1\) rows, which are skipped unread.

\subsection{Diagonal transition for near-identical pairs}

Diagonal transition extends each diagonal along its run of matches, eight letters at a time by the exclusive-or of two 64-bit words, and on AVX-512 eight diagonals together, their letters gathered under branch-free masks (Supplementary Section S1.1). The same step serves near-identical pairs, from one or both ends \citep{MarcoSola2023biwfa}, the traceback inside each tile, and the gap-affine front. A pair finished from both ends has its forward wavefronts grown on to the proven distance, kept only on the diagonals an optimal path passes, and traced from them (Section 3.1).

\subsection{Seed heuristic: direct neighbour construction}

The reference is divided into disjoint seeds of 12 bases, matched exactly, or of 16 bases, matched with at most one edit, each of whose 8-base halves indexes a table \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}; the lookups for 16 query rows are issued together, so that their cache misses overlap.

An exact match \(\mu\) of a 16-base seed at query rows \([j, j+16)\) has four neighbouring matches with one edit: two share its start, at rows \([j, j+15)\) and \([j, j+17)\), and two share its end, at \([j+1, j+16)\) and \([j-1, j+16)\). Chaining is all-or-nothing, so a neighbour may chain where \(\mu\) cannot, and the neighbours are needed for the heuristic to remain a lower bound. Rather than finding each by search and testing it for local pruning, dinara-align inserts them whenever \(\mu\) is kept, as the following lemma justifies; the search is that of local pruning (Section 2.4).

\textbf{Lemma 1.} If the search from an exact match \(\mu\) finds no path across the next \(p\) seeds, it finds none from any of its four neighbours.

\emph{Proof idea.} The search from \(\mu\) dominates that from each neighbour: at every cost and on every diagonal it reaches at least as far, and a further point has crossed at least as much potential, so it is dropped only if the nearer one is too (proof in Supplementary Section S6).

Every neighbour that the search would keep is therefore inserted. As in A*PA2, a match whose search runs into a match already kept on its diagonal is kept too. A match is dropped only if its search would find no path, which keeps the heuristic a lower bound (Lemma S1), and each further match kept can only lower it, so the alignment stays exact.

\subsection{Certified bands for inter-sequence batches}

Batches of short pairs are aligned with one pair per vector lane \citep{Rognes2011swipe,Rahn2018seqan} in saturating 8-bit lanes \citep{Zhao2013ssw,Daily2016parasail}, a saturated score computed again in 16-bit lanes. Rather than the full matrix, the lanes of a group compute the band of diagonals \([d_\ell, d_h]\) containing the main diagonal 0 and each pair's end diagonal \(\delta\), with one further diagonal on either side; pairs are grouped by end diagonal, so the band stays narrow. Its optimality is certified by a cost form of the out-of-band bounds of \citet{Gibrat2018band} and \citet{Fujiki2020seedex}, with a strict form for ties.

\textbf{Proposition 1.} Let \(C\) be the least cost of an alignment within \([d_\ell, d_h]\), and let \(L(d) = g(|d|) + g(|d-\delta|)\), or \(\infty\) for a diagonal outside the matrix. If \(C \le \min\bigl(L(d_h+1), L(d_\ell-1)\bigr)\), then \(C\) is the optimal cost; if the inequality is strict, every optimal alignment lies within the band.

\emph{Proof idea.} An alignment that leaves the band must open a gap reaching the diagonal beyond it and another returning to the end diagonal, which together cost at least \(L(d)\) for that diagonal \(d\) (proof in Supplementary Section S6).

Each lane evaluates its own certificate. When every optimal alignment lies in the band, its in-band scores are exact and the tie rule chooses as in the full matrix; pairs that fail are recomputed over every diagonal that a path at most as cheap could visit, grouped by the width of that band.

\subsection{Traceback within a memory limit}

The traceback of a band traces each tile from the boundary recorded on its left. Boundaries are kept within the alignment's memory limit, 80 MiB by default: beyond it only one in two is kept, then one in four, and so on, and each tile records the state the band carries into it, from which the traceback recomputes a stretch of tiles from the last kept boundary (Supplementary Section S1.1). A band's steps depend only on that state, so each boundary is recovered as the round left it and the alignment is the same byte for byte; splitting the pair instead, as QuickEd does \citep{Doblas2025quicked}, resolves ties within each part.

\subsection{Gap-affine and score-based alignment}

A scoring scheme with match score \(\alpha\), mismatch score \(\beta\) and gap scores \(-(o+ke)\) can be converted into costs for global alignment \citep{Eizenga2022wfalm}. Every alignment covers \(n+m\) letters, so its score \(S\) and a gap-affine cost \(C\) satisfy

\begin{equation}\begin{gathered}
S = \tfrac12\bigl(\alpha(n+m) - C\bigr),\\ C = 2(\alpha-\beta)\,X + \sum_{\text{gaps}} \bigl(2o + k(2e+\alpha)\bigr),
\end{gathered}\end{equation}

where \(X\) is the number of mismatches, so the wavefront computes score-maximising alignments. Local alignment locates the end of the optimal alignment with a forward sweep, as in SSW \citep{Zhao2013ssw}, and extends a wavefront back from it to the first cell attaining the maximal score, which avoids the correction pass that striped layouts may need \citep{Farrar2007striped}.

The wavefront keeps five bytes per diagonal for the traceback, and a pair whose fronts would exceed the memory limit is split where an optimal path crosses, as in BiWFA (Section 3.1). A global pair projected to take more work than a full sweep in 8-bit difference recurrences \citep{Suzuki2018diff} is handed to that sweep (Section 3.10), which keeps the predecessor flags of Section 3.1.

Under a substitution matrix, anti-diagonals \citep{Wozniak1997} are computed in 16-bit lanes while the scores provably fit, in strips of rows that stay in the first-level cache, and a global alignment is traced in a band of diagonals that grows until its own score proves that every optimal path lies inside it (Supplementary Section S1.4).

\subsection{One search or two at gap-affine costs}

WFA grows the wavefront from one end of the pair and keeps every front for the traceback \citep{MarcoSola2021wfa}; BiWFA grows it from both ends and keeps only the latest fronts \citep{MarcoSola2023biwfa}. Two searches must also prove where an optimal path crosses between them, so they stop only once \(2\min(s_1, s_2) \ge C^* - 1 + \theta\), where \(s_1, s_2\) are their costs, \(C^*\) the cheapest meeting found and \(\theta = o + w\) a margin: \(o\) is the largest gap-open cost and \(w = \max(x, o+e)\) the largest cost of a single edit, over both pieces for two-piece costs. Every optimal path has a cell whose costs from the two ends differ by at most \(w\), and a meeting inside a gap pays its opening once for both halves; BiWFA stops by the same margin. A score-only computation, which needs no meeting cell, stops sooner: once its best is at most one more than the highest cost to which either search has checked the other's start. With \(W(s)\) the number of diagonals a search steps to reach cost \(s\), two searches need about \(2W((C_{\mathrm{opt}}+\theta)/2)\) steps for a pair of cost \(C_{\mathrm{opt}}\), plus the setup of the second, and one search \(W(C_{\mathrm{opt}})\). Where the fronts widen with the cost, \(W(s)\) grows with \(s^2\) and one search is cheaper while \(C_{\mathrm{opt}} < (1+\sqrt2)\,\theta\); where the ends of the sequences bound the fronts, it is always cheaper. Most 250~bp Illumina reads cost less than \(\theta\), 14 at (4, 6, 2).

dinara-align therefore starts with a single search, the one whose fronts the traceback reads (the backward search under the default tie rule), keeps its fronts and traces the alignment as soon as the search reaches the far corner. Every cost \(s\) passed without reaching it shows that \(C_{\mathrm{opt}} > s\), and the search measures \(W\) as it grows: it continues alone while \(s < \theta\), costs the second search would pass in any case, and then while \(W(s) \le 2W(\lfloor (s+\theta)/2 \rfloor)\), that is, while it has stepped no more diagonals than two searches would need for the cheapest cost still possible. It also hands over at half the memory limit or when a band leaves it no reachable cell. The rule has no tuned constant: it hands over at about \(2.4\theta\) where the fronts widen with the cost, and never where the sequences bound the fronts from early costs on, where it aligns exactly as WFA does.

\textbf{Proposition 2.} Suppose the first search stops at cost \(\sigma\) without reaching the far corner, and the second search, growing from cost 0, checks each new front against the last \(w+1\) fronts of the first, costs \(\sigma-w\) to \(\sigma\), while its own cost is at most \(\sigma\), after which the two alternate as in BiWFA, each new front checked against the other side's last \(w+1\). When they stop, \(C^*\) is the optimal cost and its meeting lies on an optimal path.

\emph{Proof idea.} On every optimal path the costs from the two starts change by at most \(w\) a move, so some cell has them within \(w\) of each other, and the two phases check every such cell before the stopping rule can end the searches (proof in Supplementary Section S6).

An alignment traced from the unpruned fronts of the single search is the one the two searches would have traced: the traceback steps only from a cell to a predecessor on an optimal path, and the fronts that two searches prune hold no such cell, so the tie rule is unchanged (Supplementary Table S1 gives the effect on short reads).

\subsection{Hand-overs that wait on a runtime estimate}

Two hand-overs rest on projections of the work still needed: diagonal transition hands over to band doubling once its remaining work is projected to exceed a band's, and the gap-affine wavefront to the difference sweep once its projected total exceeds the sweep's. A projection can exceed the distance a hundredfold when edits gather at the ends, as on nanopore reads with adapters or poly-A tails, and hand a pair that the search would finish in microseconds to a band over the whole matrix. dinara-align hands over on a projection only once the work already spent has reached one twenty-fourth of the cheapest alternative that could still be needed: for diagonal transition, the band whose bound equals the cost already reached, which no band can undercut; for the wavefront, the full sweep. Once the projection favours the alternative, this delays the hand-over by at most about 4\% of the work the alternative needs in any case. An alignment's one-ended diagonal transition also waits until the projected work exceeds the band's by a factor \(1 + 1.5/\sqrt{q}\) after \(q\) edits, 1.5 times the relative error of a projection from \(q\) edits. A pair of at most 2{,}048 columns hands over on no projection: its band covers the whole matrix at a cost known in advance, so its searches give up only once their steps would have paid for that band, and it costs at most twice the cheaper of the two (Supplementary Table S1).

\subsection{Per-pair overhead on short reads}

A 250~bp read aligns in well under a microsecond, so work that does not depend on the pair dominates. An aligner object keeps every buffer its searches use from pair to pair, one aligner per thread, as each competitor's benchmark runner keeps its own; both sequences are encoded, and reversed for the leftmost tie rule, in one vectorised pass; and an aligner warms its buffers on two built-in pairs when it is made, about 80~\textmu s once, while a single call takes one that does not (Supplementary Table S1).

\subsection{Thresholds measured against the code}

The choice of algorithm and the bounds of each search rest on 41 thresholds. We built dinara-align with each halved and with each doubled and timed the 82 builds against the unchanged one: about thirty moved no sample by more than 3\%, most others traded one dataset against another, and one had become outdated, the length from which seeds match with one edit (Supplementary Section S1.1).

\subsection{Validation}

A differential fuzzer checks every mode, cost model, band, cost limit and memory limit on random pairs against a full-matrix implementation that shares no code with the library, for validity, optimality and the tie rule. A unit-cost alignment is the same byte for byte under any memory limit, and all 305 pairs of WFA2-lib's regression set give its scores in every mode it tests and its CIGARs under its tie rule (Supplementary Section S1.7); at the benchmarked commit 20{,}000 random cases and the regression set passed.
